native_result.query: How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?
native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Among black NLSY79 respondents, incarceration between 1985 and 1994 is associated with worse wealth outcomes at every baseline-wealth tier, with the damage concentrated proportionally at the bottom: jailed respondents who began with low positive wealth (<= $5,300) typically lost all of it by 1996 (median relative change -100%, ending at median $0) while comparable non-jailed respondents grew wealth roughly five-fold (+525%); in the zero-wealth tier jailed respondents accumulated essentially nothing (jailed men ~$7,900 vs ~$18,500 mean accumulation) and in the highest positive tier jailed men saw median wealth decline ~$7,000-8,000 vs a ~$12,500 gain for non-jailed peers. Sex-adjusted regressions find a significant negative jailed coefficient in every tier (p <= 0.02). In absolute dollars the shortfall grows with baseline wealth (DiD-style gaps: -1,948 / 0 / -7,770 / -14,775 across tiers), but the cross-tier interaction is not statistically significant (p = 0.07-0.17), so the tier gradient in levels is descriptive. All statements are associations, not causal effects.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspected data (12,013 rows x 6 cols, no missing values, no ID; wide format; wealth can be negative). 2) Restricted to black respondents (n=3,013; 159 jailed, 5.3%; male 9.8% vs female 1.0%). 3) Winsorized wealth levels at black-sample 1st/99th percentiles per wave (62 rows/wave affected; 31 extreme-negative rows per wave flagged, not dropped). 4) Built primary baseline (1985) tiers negative/zero/positive-low/positive-high using the median of positive 1985 wealth ($5,300) because terciles/quartiles degenerate at 0; quartile variant run as sensitivity. 5) Computed absolute changes 1985->1990 and 1985->1996, relative changes for positive baselines, and 1996 levels. 6) Compared jailed vs not-jailed within every tier x sex cell via medians, winsorized means, and Mann-Whitney U tests (both cells >= 5); reported jailed/non-jailed counts per tier x sex. 7) Pooled within-tier sex-adjusted OLS (HC3) of change 1985->1996 on jailed + male. 8) DiD-style jail gaps in change by tier and cross-tier jail x tier interaction OLS. 9) Stated associational caveats: coarse 1985-1994 ever_jailed proxy with unmeasured timing/severity; non-random selection into incarceration; unknown composite-wealth construction; no income variable so baseline wealth proxies income; tiny female jailed cells; unmeasurable attrition; possible extreme-debt coding artifacts.

sub_hypo.text: Among black NLSY79 respondents, incarceration between 1985 and 1994 is associated with worse 1985–1996 wealth outcomes in every baseline-wealth tier, including after adjustment for sex.
sub_hypo.context: Black NLSY79 respondents, stratified by 1985 wealth into negative, zero, positive-low ($0 < wealth <= $5,300), and positive-high (> $5,300) tiers; wealth levels winsorized at black-sample 1st/99th percentiles per wave.

sub_hypo.text: Among black respondents with low positive baseline wealth, jailed respondents typically lost all their wealth by 1996, whereas comparable non-jailed respondents increased their wealth substantially.
sub_hypo.context: Black NLSY79 respondents with positive 1985 wealth <= $5,300; incarceration measured over 1985–1994 and outcomes measured in 1996.
sub_hypo.relations: Jailed respondents had median relative wealth change of -100% and median 1996 wealth of $0, versus approximately +525% relative growth among non-jailed respondents. Proportional damage is concentrated at the bottom of positive baseline wealth; the association is not causal.

sub_hypo.text: Among black respondents starting with zero wealth, jailed respondents accumulated essentially nothing; jailed men accumulated about $7,900 on average versus about $18,500 among non-jailed men.
sub_hypo.context: Black NLSY79 respondents with zero 1985 wealth; numerical mean-accumulation comparison concerns men over 1985–1996.
sub_hypo.relations: Incarceration during 1985–1994 is associated with lower subsequent wealth accumulation in the zero-baseline tier, with mean accumulation among men approximately $7,900 jailed versus $18,500 non-jailed. This is not a causal effect.

sub_hypo.text: Among black men in the highest positive baseline-wealth tier, jailed respondents experienced a median wealth decline of approximately $7,000–8,000, whereas non-jailed peers gained approximately $12,500.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY79 respondents with 1985 wealth > $5,300; wealth change measured from 1985 to 1996 and incarceration over 1985–1994.
sub_hypo.relations: Jailed men had negative median absolute wealth change, contrasting with positive median change among non-jailed men in the same baseline tier. The difference is associational, not causal.

sub_hypo.text: Among black respondents, the absolute-dollar wealth shortfall associated with incarceration is descriptively larger at higher baseline wealth, but cross-tier differences are not statistically significant.
sub_hypo.context: Black NLSY79 respondents across negative, zero, positive-low (<= $5,300), and positive-high (> $5,300) 1985 wealth tiers; 1985–1996 wealth changes.
sub_hypo.relations: DiD-style jailed versus non-jailed gaps in wealth change are -$1,948, $0, -$7,770, and -$14,775 across the four ordered tiers.
